855.bp: When a company files its annual 10-K report with regulators, it must disclose what has changed in its business—new risks, strategic shifts, financial performance. Investors who want to spot trouble early need to spot these real changes, but 10-K filings are bloated with repeated legal boilerplate that hides the signal in noise. The goal is to automatically extract what actually changed year to year, so a fund manager can see a red flag (or opportunity) hiding in thousands of pages.
855.wh: The obvious move—scan a 10-K for sentiment (positive words vs. negative words)—fails badly because the filing is packed with templated risk disclaimers and standard phrasing that looks negative on paper but carries no new information. A human investor knows to ignore the boilerplate and focus only on newly disclosed or removed statements. But machines treating all negative words equally will flag the entire filing as pessimistic even when nothing substantive changed.

The core tension is that most of a 10-K is copy-pasted from last year unchanged. Analyzing the whole document treats that repetition as real signal. What actually matters is *what moved*—which sentences disappeared and which appear for the first time—because that's where genuine business changes hide.
855.ap: The paper takes a two-step approach. First, it uses neural sentence matching to align sentences from year t with year t+1, marking each as Kept (unchanged boilerplate), Deleted (removed), or Added (new). Then it computes a net sentiment shift: take the average sentiment of newly Added sentences minus the average sentiment of Deleted ones, using FinBERT (a financial-tuned sentiment model). The difference becomes a single 'Core Sentiment' score that captures whether disclosures genuinely got more or less optimistic.
855.ww: This works because it strips away the noise of repetition. By ignoring what stayed the same, you force the model to measure only real change. If a company newly discloses a legal risk (negative), that Deleted optimistic language elsewhere won't drown it out. The magnitude of the shift matters: a small positive disclosure added alongside large positive deletions signals a real pessimistic turn, which raw sentiment would hide.
855.po: The framework produces a cleaner risk signal: investors can now detect meaningful business pivots buried in annual filings, and the method outperforms standard bag-of-words sentiment on real 10-K data. This opens the door to semi-automated compliance analysis and early detection of strategic shifts before quarterly earnings calls.

856.bp: Large language models are now the main way people search and reason over web data, but they often hallucinate or contradict each other because they work from statistical pattern-matching alone. Knowledge graphs—structured databases of entities and their relationships—offer the opposite: explicitly curated facts with clear links. The goal is to combine both powers: let LLMs reason flexibly, but ground them in a structured graph so their answers stay true and explainable.
856.wh: LLMs alone are beautiful for natural conversation but unreliable for facts. Knowledge graphs are precise but rigid—they don't handle ambiguity or reasoning steps well. Putting them together is hard because LLMs generate freeform text while graphs demand structure. How do you make an LLM consult a graph mid-reasoning? How do you validate that what the LLM generated actually follows from the graph?
856.ap: GLOW (the workshop topic) focuses on architectures that weave graph structure into LLM reasoning: the LLM learns to query a knowledge graph as a retrieval step, verifies its answers against graph facts, and explains its logic by walking through explicit relationships. Instead of the LLM speaking freely, it treats the graph as a source of truth to check against, and the graph acts as a scaffold for the LLM's reasoning chain.
856.ww: Graphs provide semantic scaffolding that LLMs can lean on. When an LLM generates a claim, the graph can instantly check: 'Does this relationship exist in our curated data?' This creates a feedback loop—the LLM learns to make claims the graph will validate, and the graph fills in relational context the LLM can't derive from text alone. Transparency emerges because every reasoning step is now traceable through graph edges.
856.po: The payoff is web-scale systems that are both conversational and trustworthy. Users get natural language access to data without sacrificing accuracy or explainability. For enterprise applications (medical records, compliance, supply chains), this hybrid approach lets machines reason over messy real-world data while staying verifiable and auditable.

857.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation pairs an LLM with a search engine: the engine finds relevant documents, the LLM reads them and answers a question. This is how most chatbots avoid hallucinating on private data. The bottleneck is speed: searching through millions of documents and then feeding all their text to the LLM is slow and expensive. The dream is to compress documents down to their essential meaning so the LLM gets more signal per unit of compute.
857.wh: Naive compression (shrinking documents uniformly to save tokens) backfires. If you crush a long document equally everywhere—squeezing technical details, examples, and boilerplate at the same rate—you lose what mattered for *this specific query*. A query-agnostic compression treats a medical article the same whether someone asks about symptoms or drug interactions. The obvious math-efficient solution (autoencoders that compress everything) actually hurts the LLM's ability to answer because it discards query-relevant facts alongside noise.
857.ap: Instead of compressing every document the same way, the paper proposes SeleCom: train a small selector model to read a document *and the query together*, then output only the sentences that matter for that query. The selector learns to flag relevant passages and discard irrelevant ones, acting as a query-aware filter rather than a compression machine. Training uses synthetic Q&A pairs graded by difficulty, so the selector learns to recognize relevance at different complexity levels.
857.ww: This shifts the goal from 'make small' to 'pick what matters.' Because the selector sees both the query and document, it can spot that a medical paper's symptom section is relevant for one user but irrelevant for another asking about side effects. Smaller output happens as a side effect of this precision filtering, not at the expense of information density. The selector learns task-specific relevance rather than generic compression.
857.po: SeleCom matches or beats standard RAG (which uses full documents) while slashing context size and latency. This makes RAG practical for resource-constrained applications and enables faster, cheaper LLM reasoning at scale. The synthetic training dataset can be adapted to new domains, making the approach reusable.

858.bp: Current spam filters, fake news detectors, and grammar checkers work at the document level: they say 'this email is spam' or 'this review is fake' but don't show *where* in the text the problem is. For real-world applications, a user needs to know which sentence to rewrite, which phrase is suspicious, which part of a message triggered the alarm. The goal is fine-grained anomaly detection—pinpointing exactly which words or phrases are out of place.
858.wh: Document-level analysis is too coarse because a fake review might be 95% legitimate sentences with just a few planted promotional words. Global pattern-matching models trained on 'spam vs. not spam' miss local weirdness because they average over everything. And most anomaly datasets only label documents, not individual words, so training fine-grained detectors is impossible without manual annotation.
858.ap: The paper introduces token-level anomaly detection: instead of labeling a whole document, they annotated three datasets (spam, reviews, grammar errors) word-by-word to mark which tokens are anomalous. Then they built a unified framework that can operate at both document and token levels—predicting not just 'is this text wrong' but 'which parts are wrong and why' (spam keywords, fake review markers, grammatical errors).
858.ww: By training on token-level labels, the model learns to recognize that a few specific phrases like 'act now' or 'limited offer' are red flags in reviews, while the same phrase in a marketing email is normal. Word-level supervision teaches the model to spot inconsistency and deviation in context, not just global oddness. The dual-level approach lets it generalize: a spam detector trained this way can also flag suspicious passages in other domains.
858.po: Annotated benchmarks now exist for token-level anomaly detection, enabling precise, explainable content moderation. A spam filter can tell a user exactly which words got it flagged. A grammar checker can highlight the specific error. Suspicious reviews can be examined word-by-word, making moderation decisions auditable and helping users fix problems rather than just reject content.

859.bp: Federated learning lets thousands of organizations train an AI model together without sharing raw data—each site trains on its own data, sends only model updates to a central server. This is crucial for sensitive domains like healthcare and finance. But federated learning is vulnerable to poisoning: a bad actor can send malicious updates to sabotage the global model. Recent work moved to ranking-based federated learning (FRL), which only communicates discrete rankings instead of continuous numbers, making poisoning harder. The question is: can adversaries still attack ranking-based systems in new ways?
859.wh: Traditional federated learning poisoning is easy to spot—malicious updates look extreme and get filtered out. Ranking-based FRL was designed to be robust because rankings are discrete; you can't smoothly optimize an attack in the continuous space. But the researchers found a blind spot: an attacker can still manipulate which rankings win, creating a fine-grained control attack that looks normal on the surface while secretly degrading specific models—like silently crippling a competitor's accuracy while maintaining the appearance of normal convergence.
859.ap: The Edge Control Attack (ECA) works in two stages. First, the attacker maps the global model update process to understand which discrete ranking 'edges' (comparisons between model versions) drive convergence. Then they craft local poisoned data that inverts specific edges—making the global model prefer slightly worse directions that favor an attacker's target. Unlike blunt denial-of-service attacks that crash the model, ECA drifts the update direction incrementally, avoiding statistical red flags.
859.ww: ECA succeeds because discrete rankings hide continuous manipulation. By flipping small edge comparisons, the attacker exploits the ranking system's trust in majority vote. The global model thinks it's improving (it's following the consensus direction) but actually slides toward a poisoned target. Detection is hard because the convergence curve looks normal—the model improves, just not as well as it should, and that gap is easy to miss.
859.po: The paper reveals that ranking-based federated learning, while more robust than traditional FL, is not immune to sophisticated attacks. This motivates new defenses tailored to ranking-based systems (e.g., Byzantine-robust ranking aggregation). The work pushes federated learning security forward and shows that moving to discrete representations doesn't eliminate adversarial risk—it only changes the attack surface.

860.bp: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain millions of medical codes and concepts—diagnoses, procedures, medications. Each one currently gets a separate numerical representation (an embedding) stored in memory. As hospitals scale, this balloons into gigabytes of tables. The deeper problem: these embeddings ignore the natural hierarchy of medicine (pneumonia is a type of respiratory infection, which is a type of infection) so models miss the semantic structure that doctors use to reason. The goal is to compress medical concepts while preserving hierarchical meaning.
860.wh: Naive compression (squashing medical codes into smaller vectors) destroys hierarchy. You lose the fact that appendicitis and hepatitis are both inflammatory conditions. Recent work tried to encode concepts as discrete codes (like codebooks), which saves memory, but treats every concept independently—a flat assignment rather than a layered one. A model trained on this discrete flat representation can't leverage the medical ontology structure that would help it generalize to new procedures or unseen diseases.
860.ap: MedRQ (ontology-driven residual vector quantization) treats the medical hierarchy as a scaffold. Instead of assigning each concept a single discrete code, it assigns sequences of codes that align with multi-level medical ontologies. A code at level 1 might represent 'infection,' level 2 'respiratory infection,' level 3 'pneumonia.' During training, the model is supervised to generate codes consistent with this hierarchy. Residual quantization means each level adds detail to the previous level's representation.
860.ww: Hierarchical supervision teaches the model to cluster concepts meaningfully: if two diseases are siblings in the ontology, their code sequences should be similar. This forces the model to learn that appendicitis and gastroenteritis are both GI inflammation, which helps predict complications or drug interactions across similar conditions. The hierarchy acts as an inductive bias—the model doesn't have to discover these relationships from scratch; it's built into the training signal.
860.po: MedRQ shrinks memory overhead dramatically while improving prediction on clinical tasks (patient deterioration, readmission risk). Clinicians also gain interpretability: the multi-level codes reveal *why* the model makes a prediction. A model that groups a rare disease with known common cousins can generalize to unseen diagnoses, which is crucial in healthcare where true novel cases appear regularly.

861.bp: Recommender systems on shopping sites need to instantly suggest relevant items from millions of candidates. A two-stage approach is standard: first narrow down to 100s using fast math (e.g., inner product of user/item vectors), then re-rank the top candidates with a heavier model. The bottleneck in the narrow-down stage (retrieval) is that simple math doesn't capture why a user likes an item. The question is: how do you make retrieval smarter—capturing richer preference signals—without blowing up latency?
861.wh: Traditional item-to-item collaborative filtering recommends items similar to what the user liked. But 'similarity' is often measured by inner product, which only catches surface-level patterns. A user who bought a phone case and a laptop sleeve might not want a laptop bag, even though all three are accessories. The truncation step that pre-filters the item pool also bleeds quality: if you aggressively cut items to stay fast, you discard borderline candidates that might be perfect for some users but not others. One-size-fits-all filtering wastes personalization.
861.ap: PI2I uses two stages. First, an 'Indexer Building Stage' relaxes the truncation threshold—keep more candidate items initially, trading speed for recall. Second, a 'Personalized Retrieval Stage' deploys an interactive scoring model that replaces simple inner product with learned interactions. Instead of computing score = user_vector · item_vector, the model learns to reason: 'This user liked X; does Y play a similar role?' The model is trained on negative samples built from trigger-target relationships (items a user would engage with given their history), ensuring training and real-world behavior align.
861.ww: Keeping more candidates upfront ensures good items don't get filtered prematurely. The interactive scoring model then decides which matter for *this user*, using richer signals than raw similarity. By training on items the user would realistically consider next (trigger-target pairs), the model learns true preference structure—not just 'similar' but 'similar *and* aligned with their journey.' Deployed on Taobao, this beats rigid truncation strategies.
861.po: PI2I achieved a 1.05% online uplift in transaction rates at Taobao scale. For e-commerce, that translates to millions in incremental revenue. The framework is reusable: any domain with millions of items (streaming, social feeds, job boards) benefits from personalized retrieval that combines precision and speed.

862.bp: AI systems now ingest mixed media—text, images, audio, video, sensor streams. Making sense of what's happening requires both AI reasoning and visual explanation so humans trust the output. A healthcare AI that flags a scan as concerning is useless without showing the doctor *which part of the scan* it saw as anomalous. The goal is to build tools that combine multimodal AI reasoning (the compute) with interactive web visualization (the explanation) so humans and machines can collaborate.
862.wh: Multimodal AI models are blackboxes: they fuse images and text and produce a prediction, but don't explain their reasoning. Classical visualization tools are built for single modalities (text analytics, image annotation) and don't align across image, audio, and video streams. Web platforms today are siloed—speech systems live in isolation, image understanding lives elsewhere. Building an integrated system requires stitching together incompatible pieces.
862.ap: AAIMVT (the workshop) brings together four concrete applications: a privacy-preserving voice-cloning platform with unified web UI (users upload speech, customize tone, retrieve output); a cybersecurity ontology tool that bridges policies and operations via interactive web graphs; a harmful-meme detector that works even when modalities are missing (no image, only text); and infographic reconstruction that parses static graphics back into structured data. Each uses the web as the integration layer.
862.ww: Web interfaces are the connective tissue. Because they run in browsers, they're platform-agnostic: a voice-cloning system, a cybersecurity ontology, and a meme detector can all live in the same application. The browser also handles UI composition naturally—you can show audio waveforms, graph visualizations, image annotations, and text explanations side-by-side. This makes multimodal systems feel coherent to users.
862.po: The workshop surfaced working systems that combine applied AI with visualization, proving that web-native tooling accelerates deployment. Voice privacy, cybersecurity governance, content moderation, and data extraction all became tractable through integrated web platforms. The patterns established here—unified UIs for heterogeneous modalities, browser-as-platform—are now reusable templates for other multimodal AI applications.

863.bp: Federated learning is how hospitals, power plants, and manufacturing sites train AI without uploading sensitive data to the cloud. But the traditional approach—each site sends model parameter updates to a central server—is slow (lots of data) and leaky (adversaries can reverse-engineer raw data from gradients). Recent work uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to avoid sending parameters at all—sites send only semantic knowledge extracted from their data. The challenge is diagnosing rare equipment failures across sites that have sparse examples and strict privacy rules.
863.wh: Long-tail faults (rare but critical failures) are hard anywhere. In federated settings, they're doubly hard: one site might have zero examples of a failure, another site has three, scattered across time. Traditional federated learning struggles because gradients computed from scarce samples are noisy (gradient starvation). Gradient inversion attacks can also extract raw data from those updates. Multimodal data (vibration signals + thermal readings) adds complexity—aligning different sensor types across sites is non-trivial.
863.ap: Fed-S2 abandons parameter sharing entirely. Instead, each site builds local semantic embeddings of its sensor data (vibrations, temperature, sound), sanitizes them via 'Semantic Shielding' (a privacy technique), and uploads only those lightweight vectors to a central knowledge graph. The server constructs a global graph connecting these embeddings across sites. At inference time, when a new fault pattern arrives, the system performs retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve similar past faults from the graph, then use a frozen LLM to reason about what the new fault most likely is, even with zero prior examples.
863.ww: Embeddings are privacy-safer than gradients because they're task-specific, not raw data. The adversarial game (min-max optimization under information-bottleneck bounds) ensures that inversion attacks yield noise, not reconstructed signals. Frequency-domain alignment handles multimodal sensor fusion—different modalities are aligned in spectral space before embedding, so vibration and temperature data integrate naturally. The frozen LLM acts as a universal reasoner, generalizing across sites without retraining.
863.po: Fed-S2 improves long-tail fault identification from 38.5% to 84.2% and achieves 68.5% zero-shot accuracy on new fault types where traditional federated learning fails entirely (0%). It cuts communication by 93% compared to standard parameter-sharing FL. For critical infrastructure, this means faster fault detection, lower bandwidth, and provable privacy—enabling real-world deployment where lives and infrastructure depend on it.

864.bp: The Web evolves: pages change, links break, new content appears, trends rise and fall. Understanding these temporal dynamics—how information spreads, how topics evolve, how institutions adapt—requires studying the Web through time. But most tools treat the Web as a static snapshot. The goal is to build infrastructure for temporal web analytics: tools to archive the Web, query it across years, and spot patterns that only emerge over time—like suicide risk signals rising in online communities.
864.wh: Querying the temporal Web is hard because there's no unified standard for time-aware queries. Do you want pages as they appeared on January 1, 2020? All edits in 2021? The intersection of two events across different websites? Web archives (like the Internet Archive) exist but are queried via full-text search, not structured temporal queries. Scaling analysis to millions of pages across decades requires infrastructure that doesn't yet exist.
864.ap: TempWeb (the 16th workshop) covers the full spectrum: temporal information extraction (finding when events occurred in text), temporal information retrieval (retrieving documents from specific time periods), web archiving infrastructure (building queryable historical snapshots), and large-scale temporal data analysis. Contributions range from benchmarks for temporal reasoning to applications like early detection of suicide risk by monitoring linguistic shifts in online forums.
864.ww: Temporal structure reveals causality and emergent phenomena that snapshots miss. If you see suicide-risk language rising in a forum over weeks before an incident, you can intervene. If you track how a company's web presence evolved over years, you spot business pivots. The temporal dimension turns the Web from a static knowledge base into a living historical record where patterns unfold over time.
864.po: The workshop established temporal analytics as a first-class citizen in Web research. Contributors now have benchmarks for temporal IE/IR tasks, infrastructure recommendations for archiving and querying temporal data, and validated applications (health monitoring, platform safety, Web evolution studies). This enables research that was previously impossible—understanding long-term dynamics, detecting early warning signals, and learning how the Web transforms.

865.bp: Building predictive models on tabular data (spreadsheets of customer records, sensor readings, financial data) requires feature engineering—combining raw columns into new ones that the model can leverage. A machine learning engineer might spend weeks crafting features by hand: ratios, aggregations, domain-specific combinations. The dream is automatic feature engineering: let an AI system discover useful features without human guidance. But traditional automated approaches generate code blindly, making mistakes that are hard to debug.
865.wh: LLMs are amazing at code generation, but when they generate entire features from scratch, edits are coarse-grained. If an LLM writes 'new_feature = log(abs(X1) + 1)' and you ask it to tweak this, it might rewrite it entirely rather than adjusting just the log or the absolute value. Without a structured representation, it's hard to enforce constraints (feature must be positive, must fit in memory, must preserve causality). This makes the search space chaotic and features hard to interpret.
865.ap: AFE-Master uses a domain-specific language (DSL) to represent features as abstract syntax trees (ASTs)—structured recipes instead of free-form code. A feature like 'log(abs(X1) + 1)' becomes a tree node: log(abs(sum(X1, const=1))). The LLM now manipulates this tree, making targeted edits: swap the log for exp, replace sum with multiply, push the constant to a different branch. A guided local search explores nearby variants, keeping only edits that improve model performance. The structure also lets you enforce semantic constraints (no division by zero, features must decompose hierarchically).
865.ww: Trees make edits traceable and composable. Because features are hierarchical, you can reason about what each layer contributes. Swapping a logarithm for an exponential has a clear semantic effect (compression vs. amplification). Guided local search then finds efficient paths through the space—instead of randomly sampling features, it follows gradients through syntactic neighbors. Interpretability emerges because every feature is a readable tree, not a black-box mutation.
865.po: AFE-Master discovers information-dense, human-readable features faster than traditional evolutionary approaches. On Kaggle and OpenML benchmarks, it outperforms both automatic feature generators and human-designed baselines. Practitioners get features they can explain to stakeholders, and the DSL makes the search process auditable—you can see every transformation the LLM proposed and accepted.

866.bp: Dense retrieval (searching by semantic meaning rather than keywords) powers modern search engines and RAG systems. But these neural retrieval models—fine-tuned transformers that compare queries and documents—can be fooled by adversarial tricks: add a few planted sentences to a document and the model might rank it as relevant even when it's not. Worse, users have no idea *which part* of a document actually matched their query. The goal is robust retrieval that resists attacks and explains its decisions.
866.wh: Dense models rely on learned patterns and are vulnerable to data poisoning. If someone adds a phrase like 'Barack Obama was born in Kenya' to a document, a retrieval model might rank it highly for any query mentioning Obama, even though the sentence is false and unrelated. Adversarial attacks are easy to craft and hard to detect because the model treats all parts of a document equally. Models also lack explainability—they return a relevance score with no indication of *why*.
866.ap: The paper uses counterfactual analysis borrowed from causal reasoning. Train the retrieval model to be sensitive to key passages: if removing a passage drops the relevance score sharply, that passage is truly relevant; if removing filler has little effect, it's noise. They formalize this as a game where the model tries to produce high variance for key passages and low variance for filler, using unsupervised counterfactual passages (synthetically generated variants of documents with key phrases swapped out or removed).
866.ww: Sensitivity to key passages makes the model robust. An adversary who adds a planted sentence now faces a problem: if they sneak in 'Obama born in Kenya' to push relevance up, the model learns to be indifferent to it (low variance when removed). Over time, the model learns to weight genuine relevance signals and ignore planted text. Counterfactuals force this learning without labeled adversarial examples—the model discovers robustness by practicing on synthetically perturbed documents.
866.po: Counterfactual-trained retrievers resist adversarial attacks better than standard models, and their variance structure lets you extract which passages actually influenced the ranking—enabling explainability. Users can see 'your query matched these three sentences in the document,' making the model's decision auditable. On IR benchmarks, the approach maintains performance while improving robustness and transparency.

867.bp: Causal reasoning is how humans understand the world: why did sales drop? What caused the equipment failure? Which policy change drove unemployment? But reasoning over knowledge graphs (databases of interconnected facts) is hard because graphs are messy—data is incomplete, entities have multiple names, relationships are indirect. The goal is to do causal reasoning *directly over knowledge graphs* rather than extracting flat data first, enabling reasoning on incomplete, heterogeneous information.
867.wh: Standard causal frameworks assume flat, fully observed data. Real knowledge graphs violate every assumption: entities are heterogeneous (people, products, events), relationships are multi-relational (X owns Y, X employs Z, Y depends on Z), and data is incomplete (we don't know all facts). Causal discovery (learning which variables cause which) becomes impossible without ontological grounding—how do you know if a missing fact is truly absent or just unobserved? Causal inference also breaks because relational dependencies between entities violate independence assumptions.
867.ap: The thesis proposes CauseKG, SemMatch, HyKG-CF, and BaLu—an end-to-end pipeline. CauseKG integrates ontological semantics: represent causal relationships as typed edges aligned with domain ontologies (medical, financial). SemMatch handles entity disambiguation and resolution. HyKG-CF performs counterfactual prediction: given a graph, reason about what would change if we perturb an entity or relationship. BaLu aggregates results across graph fragments under the Open World Assumption (unobserved facts may exist). Together, they enable query-based causal reasoning.
867.ww: Ontological types ground causality. A relationship 'drug X causes symptom Y' means something different from 'gene X causes disease Y'—the semantics differ. By anchoring to ontologies, you encode domain knowledge into the causal structure. Counterfactual prediction over subgraphs then becomes tractable: to ask 'would lowering a patient's sodium cause a better outcome,' you simulate the graph perturbation using learned causal rules specific to medical ontology.
867.po: The pipeline enables causal intelligence over messy real-world data. Hospitals can reason about patient outcomes. Economists can model policy effects. Supply chain managers can trace failure cascades. Each domain gets domain-aware causal reasoning without rewriting the machinery. The framework unifies causal discovery (learning what causes what), causal inference (estimating effects), and counterfactual reasoning (simulating alternatives), making causal analysis accessible on knowledge graphs.

868.bp: Peer review is how science validates itself—experts read papers and decide what's worth publishing. But reviewers are human: they miss details, write careless comments, sometimes contradict each other. The goal is to build systems that audit peer reviews at scale: check whether reviews are thorough and factual, whether reviewers actually engaged with the paper, and whether conclusions are backed by evidence. This supports better journals and helps emerging researchers understand why their work was rejected.
868.wh: Assessing review quality is subjective. What makes a review 'good'? Is it specific (mentions particular equations, figures) or vague (generic feedback)? Is the tone constructive or dismissive? How do you verify that a reviewer's criticisms are actually supported by the paper? Expert humans can judge this reliably, but there are millions of reviews every year. Automating this requires understanding both the review text and the underlying paper—a hard task that tests LLM reasoning and grounding.
868.ap: The work builds two systems. First, a review-quality assessment module that evaluates reviews on dimensions like specificity and tone, comparing zero-shot LLM predictions against expert-annotated benchmarks. Second, a factual verification module that takes a reviewer's claim (e.g., 'the authors use dataset X') and checks whether the paper supports it by retrieving relevant sections and matching. They compare static metrics (text length, readability), machine learning baselines, zero-shot LLMs, and fine-tuned models.
868.ww: Combining natural language assessment with retrieval-based verification provides multiple signals. An LLM is good at understanding intent ('this review is dismissive'), while retrieval + matching is good at factual grounding ('this claim has textual support'). Hybrid approaches outperform LLMs alone because they anchor language understanding in evidence. The benchmarks ground evaluation in human expert judgment, so you can measure progress objectively.
868.po: Deployable systems for auditing reviews at scale enable new accountability in peer review. Journal editors can prioritize reviews for deeper inspection, authors understand whether criticisms are supported, and systems can flag potentially unfair or shallow reviews. This infrastructure supports research integrity—not replacing human reviewers, but augmenting them with systems that catch low-quality feedback and surface fairness issues.

869.bp: Granger causality is a statistical method for discovering cause-and-effect from time series: if variable X's past values help predict variable Y better than Y's history alone, then X probably causes Y. This is how economists detect policy effects on markets, how doctors diagnose patient deterioration, and how manufacturers spot equipment failures. But time series are messy—data has outliers, multiple scales, and context (a spike might be seasonal, not causal). The goal is to improve causal discovery by enriching time series with semantic context from language models.
869.wh: Raw time series are context-blind. A temperature spike looks the same whether caused by a broken sensor, a maintenance event, or external weather. Granger causality methods find statistical relationships but can't distinguish spurious correlation from true causality without domain knowledge. LLMs encode world knowledge—'temperature rises seasonally in summer'—but they work on text, not numbers. Bridging the gap requires converting time series to semantic space where an LLM can reason about context.
869.ap: LLM-GC encodes time series and text simultaneously. For each time series (e.g., stock price, patient vitals), generate semantic descriptions using an LLM ('stock price rose 5% amid economic optimism'). Then align temporal features (numerical trends) with semantic features (text descriptions) using cross-modal retrieval. A causality-aware self-attention mechanism (inverted from standard attention) highlights causal patterns that appear consistently in both modalities. The model learns that if numerical causality (X predicts Y in numbers) aligns with semantic causality (descriptions support the relationship), it's a robust causal link.
869.ww: Multimodal fusion disambiguates spurious patterns. A numerical correlation between two time series might be coincidence, but if semantic descriptions align ('both increased due to regulation'), it becomes credible causality. The inverted attention mechanism forces the model to attend to causal patterns explicitly, filtering out noise. LLMs as semantic priors inject domain knowledge—the model learns faster because it doesn't derive all context from scarce data.
869.po: LLM-GC outperforms existing Granger causality methods on synthetic and real benchmarks. Applications gain speed and accuracy: faster diagnosis of equipment faults, more reliable detection of policy effects on markets, better understanding of disease progression. The framework is the first bridge between LLMs and causal discovery, opening new hybrid methods that combine statistical rigor with semantic reasoning.
